If heavy bleeding, stabilize patient and consider transfusion. C

Colonoscopy is the initial diagnostic test, but it does not need to be pursued urgently in most circumstances. C

A diverticulum (pleural form: diverticula) is a herniation of the mucosal and submucosal wall away from the bowel lumen through defects in the muscle. These defects are usually located where blood vessels pierce the muscle wall.
Diverticular bleeding occurs from injury to arteries supplying colonic diverticula.
Incidence is 10% in patients <40 years of age and 50% to 66% in patients >80 years of age.
The bleeding risk in patients with asymptomatic diverticulosis is 0.5 per 1000 person-years.

Based on a national hospital database, authors of one study reported that age-adjusted incidence rates of colonic diverticular bleeding were decreasing from 30.4/100,000 in 2001 to 23.9/100,000 in 2009.
Prevalence of diverticulosis is 20 to 100 per 1000 in autopsy and barium enema series in 1920 to 1940.

Diverticular bleeding is the source of 17% to 40% of lower gastrointestinal bleeding. In a study of 2528 cases of lower GI bleeding prospectively reported by 143 hospitals in the United Kingdom, diverticular bleeding was the most common diagnosis occurring in 26.4%.
Life-threatening diverticular hemorrhage occurred in 3.1% of patients in one study.
In a study of massive lower GI bleeding in 50 patients, arteriography revealed a source in 36 patients (72%); 19 were caused from diverticular disease and 15 from arteriovenous malformations.
Ninety percent of diverticula are left-sided in Western societies.
Right-sided diverticula more common in Asian populations.
Estimated hospital admission rate for lower GI bleeding is 20 patients per 100,000 admissions.
Yearly mortality rate is 2.5 per 100,000 per year.

Left colon accounts for most diverticulitis while right accounts for majority of bleeding in 50% to 90% of patients. In one cohort study, the presence of right diverticula was more frequent in patients admitted for diverticular bleeding than in patients referred for colonoscopy who had no bleeding (65.2% vs. 32.4%).
Probably multifactorial, including alteration in colonic wall resistance, in colonic motility and/or in the composition of bacterial flora.

According to the Health Professionals Follow-Up Study, the risk of diverticulitis was highest among men in the highest quintile of Western dietary pattern score of high in red meat, refined grains, and high-fat dairy (hazard ratio [HR] 1.55; 95% CI 1.20-1.99). Conversely, high vs. low prudent scores, a diet high in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains, were associated with decreased risk of diverticulitis (HR 0.74; 95% CI 0.60-0.91).
The role of dietary factors (i.e., lack of fiber) in diverticular bleeding is unclear.
Erosion of blood vessels in diverticula which may develop from weakness in colonic muscle wall at the site of penetrating arteries (vasa recta) through the muscularis layer.
Bleeding occurs when the artery within the diverticulum ruptures into the colonic lumen in its course through the dome of the diverticulum.

High-fiber diet is associated with decreased risk of developing diverticular disease and is recommended to prevent its progression. B
There is no clear association between consumption of nuts and popcorn and diverticular bleed. C

Suspect diverticular beeding in case of abrupt painless rectal bleeding. C
Obtain vital signs and orthostatics, hemoglobin, hematocrit, abdominal exam, and rectal exam, type and cross match 2 to 4 units of packed red blood cells. C

Diagnostic tests include in order of priority: colonoscopy in hemodynamically stable patients, CT angiogram in hemodynamically unstable patients, and exploratory laparotomy in patients with uncontrolled bleeding.C

Mucosal tear associated with sharp, tearing pain and bright red rectal bleeding
Can be painfull and itchy, is associated with bowel movements and bright red rectal bleeding

list.listitem: Initial evaluation should include a complete history and examination, vital signs, and orthostatics.
Medications should be reviewed to determine the presence of NSAIDs, antiplatelets, and anticoagulants.
Hallmark symptom is painless rectal bleeding (hematochezia), usually self-limited. Abdominal pain or discomfort is almost never present.
Mild abdominal cramping or the urge to defecate may occur due to blood in the colon.
Stool may be dark maroon color to bright red and is often mixed with gelatinous clot.
A history of peptic ulcer disease, decompensated liver cirrhosis, and epigastric tenderness, however, may indicate an upper gastrointestinal bleed (UGIB).
Vital signs may be stable if bleeding has stopped, or the patient may be hypotensive or tachycardiac if bleeding is persistent and severe.
Severe postural dizziness, postural blood pressure decrease of 20 mm Hg, or postural pulse increase of 30 beats per minute are accurate indicators of significant acute blood loss.
Patients with acute blood loss may also experience confusion, weakness, dry mucous membranes, or dry and furrowed tongue.
Abdominal exam shows active bowel sounds with no tenderness or mass.
Rectal exam may show gross blood.
Normal hemoglobin and hematocrit does not rule out GI bleeding.

About 10% to 15% of patients with hematochezia have an UGIB as a source. Nasogatric tube passage has poor sensitivity in establishing an UGIB and routine placement to rule this out is not recommended. Increased BUN/Cr ratio >18 is also suggestive of an upper GI source. A clinical suspicion of an UGIB based on history and laboratory findings should lead to an urgent EGD instead of a colonoscopy if the pre-test probability is high.

Colonoscopy should be used to identify the bleeding source and to exclude cancer. Colonoscopy is the initial diagnostic procedure of choice, but this does not need to be completed within the first 24 hours of presentation according to ACG guidelines. Rapid oral purge with oral electrolyte solution has been found safe and effective. Diagnostic yield of colonoscopy is 69% to 80%.

Active bleeding, visible vessel, or pigmented protuberance is visualized in 10% to 20% of colonoscopy examinations done for diverticular bleeding, but when present are associated with a high risk of continued or recurrent bleeding.

In one study of 52 consecutive patients with colonic diverticular bleeding who were able to undergo both contrast-enhanced CT and colonoscopy, the detection rate of bleeding by CT was 15.4% (8/52) and 38.5% by total colonoscopy. The overall detection rate for both procedures was 46.2% (24/52), which was superior to either test alone.

In another study of 442 patients with acute-onset hematochezia, CT contrast extravasation rate was 24.7% among the 202 patients with colonic diverticular bleeding and five of nine (55.6%) among patients who underwent CT within 1 hour of the last hematochezia. Extravasation at CT predicted stigmata of recent diverticular hemorrhage during colonoscopy with a sensitivity of 38 of 66 (57.6%; 95% CI 44.8- 69.7) and a specificity of 124 of 136 (91.2%; 95% CI 85.1-95.4).

Radionuclide imaging with technetium-99m-tagged red blood cells is a non-invasive test that can detect bleeding as low as 0.1 mL/min. Consider in patients with ongoing bleeding for whom colonoscopy has failed to localize and control bleeding. Radionuclide imaging provides information on the anatomic site of bleeding. Radionuclide imaging allows for repeated scanning up to 48 hours and can detect intermittent bleeding. Many centers use this test as a screening test prior to arteriography to allow for selection of a specific artery for injection. In lower GI bleeding, the likelihood of a positive scan is 51% to 59%, a positive scan has an accuracy of 75% to 97%. However, this test is not readily available in most facilities.

CTA is the initial diagnostic test in patients with ongoing hemodynamically-significant hematochezia. However, CTA is of low yield in patients with minor lower GIB or those in whom bleeding has clinically subsided. A metanalysis of 14 observational studies showed that a CTA has a sensitivity and specificity of 90% and 92%, respectively, in diagnosing the source of a lower GIB. Disadvantages include exposure to radiation and iodinated contrast, and negative results can occur if there is no active bleeding .

Although RBC scintigraphy has a relatively longer duration of study, this test is less precise in localizing the site of the bleed as compared to CTA. Also, it has a weaker correlation with transcatheter arteriography when compared to CTA for assessing lower GI bleed in both stable and hemodynamically unstable patients.As such, RBC scintigraphy has a diminishing role and should only be used when CTA is unavailable or contraindicated.

Surgical intervention should be considered in patients with large transfusion requirements, recurrent hemorrhage refractory or not amenable to other therapy, or hemodynamic instability that does not respond to medical therapy.
See for an overview of the advantages and disadvantages of different tests for lower GI bleeding.

Risk stratification tools such as the Oakland score can help identify low risk-patients appropriate for outpatient work up (Oakland score <8). These tools should however supplement and not replace clinical judgement.
The ABC risk score accurately predicts mortality after upper or lower GI bleed.
Patients typically present with painless rectal bleeding.
Assess vital signs and orthostatic vital signs.
Initial laboratory evaluation includes coagulation studies; measurement of hemoglobin, hematocrit, and serum electrolyte levels; and determination of blood urea nitrogen-to-creatinine ratio.

Admission to the intensive care unit is recommended if the patient has significant comorbid conditions, has postural blood pressure changes despite initial fluid resuscitation, remains hemodynamically unstable, or requires transfusion following initial resuscitative measures.
Patients should be typed and crossmatched for packed red blood cells, and transfusion initiated .

Stabilize patient with volume resuscitation and transfusion with packed RBCs if hemoglobin is <= 7 mg/dl (or <= 8 mg/dl if the patient has a cardiovascular disease) based on the severity of the patient's clinical situation and comorbidities.
Transfuse platelets to maintain platelet count >30,000; transfusion to >50,000 should be considered if endoscopic interventions are planned.

Consider reversal of anticoagulation in patients with life threatening bleed on vitamin K antagonist or direct acting oral anticoagulants.Transfuse platelets to maintain platelet count >30,000; transfusion to >50,000 should be considered if endoscopic interventions are planned.
For patients presenting with severe hematochezia, the possibility of an upper GI bleed should be considered and an upper endoscopy performed if the pre-test probability is high.
Consult a gastroenterologist or surgeon for urgent colonoscopy; if the diagnosis is unclear, other options include radionuclide imaging, arteriography, and surgical intervention.
See for an overview of the suggested diagnostic evaluation ().
Management consists of: (1) initial evaluation, resuscitation, and stabilization, (2) localization of bleeding site, and (3) management of bleeding. C

Not all patients require inpatient management. In patients presenting with self-limited bleeding and no adverse clinical features, an Oakland score <= 8 can be used to guide the clinician's decision to discharge for outpatient evaluation. C
A therapeutic colonoscopy may be used to treat bleeding if the source is identified. C
Patients who are hemodynamically unstable or with suspected active bleed should undergo CTA before endoscopic or radiologic treatment to localize the site of bleeding. B
Consider arteriography with embolization. C
Consider surgery if ongoing bleeding or transfusion ≥4 units packed red blood cells.C

A propensity score matched analysis of 30,526 pairs of Japanese patients compared outcomes in those treated with tranexemic acid with those not treated. There was non difference in mortality but treatment with tranexemic acid was associated with lower rates of requiring transfusion and severe bleeding events, and shorter length of stay.

Reversal of Vitamin K antagonists is suggested for patients with life threatening bleed and INR substantially above therapeutic range;; in this case, 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate is preferred to fresh frozen plasma.
In hemodynamically stable patients with no cardiovascular disease, restrictive blood transfusion is favored with a hemoglobin threshold of <=7g/dl prompting red blood cell transfusion.

In hemodynamically stable patient with acute or chronic cardiovascular disease, a more liberal red blood cell transfusion strategy should be used, with a hemoglobin threshold <= 8g/dl prompting red cell transfusion.

Platelets should be administered in the setting of severe bleed to maintain a platelet count of >30 × 109/L, and a higher threshold of >50 × 109/L can be considered if endoscopic procedures are required.
ACG guidelines (2023) recommend that in patients with diverticular hemorrhage, discontinue non-aspirin NSAIDs after hospitalization.
Discontinue aspirin for primary cardiovascular prevention after hospitalization for diverticular hemorrhage.
Continue aspirin for secondary cardiovascular prevention after hospitalization for diverticular hemorrhage.
Reevaluate the risks versus benefits of continuing non-aspirin antiplatelets, such as P2Y12 receptor antagonists, in a multidisciplinary setting after hospitalization for diverticular hemorrhage.
Surgery is rarely required because 86% of cases of diverticular bleeding can be managed by nonsurgical means.
Surgery for diverticular bleeding is indicated when the bleeding does not stop spontaneously and can't be controlled with endoscopic and angiographic interventions.
In a retrospective study of 73 patients with diverticular bleeding, 14% required urgent colectomy and 8% required total abdominal colectomy because the bleeding site could not be localized.
The mortality rate for urgent colectomy done for diverticular bleeding is 20%.

Consider surgery with large transfusion requirements (>4 units of packed RBCs), recurrent bleeding not amenable to nonsurgical therapy, or hemodynamic instability that does not respond to medical treatment.
The surgical procedure of choice is directed segmental resection if a bleeding site has been localized.
A subtotal colectomy may be considered if bleeding can not be localized or managed by nonsurgical methods.

However, partial colectomy after preoperative localization is associated with perioperative morbidity of 8.6% compared with 37% when emergent subtotal colectomy is performed for those without preoperative localization.
Laparoscopic sigmoid resection is associated with shorter hospital stays and lower post-operative complications than open sigmoid resection.
Consider elective surgery after second bleeding episode.

High-dose barium enema has been reported to stop bleeding in cases where the source is not detected; in one case series of 57 patients, this treatment solely stopped bleeding in 11 cases and decreased recurrent bleeding similar to endoscopic hemostasis (about half in both groups).

In another Japanese RCT of 54 patients hospitalized with diverticular bleeding who had spontaneous cessation of bleeding, fewer of those randomized to high dose barium enema had bleeding recurrence at 1-year (15% vs. 43% in the conservative treatment group).

Endoscopic treatment modalities for diverticular bleed include thermal contact therapy (usually used in combination with injection of epinephrine), endoscopic ligation (through-the-scope or cap-mounted), endoscopic band ligation (EBL) Considering long-term outcomes, EBL might be the best available option for endoscopic hemostasis.
Endoscopic therapy may be applied if active bleeding, visible vessel, or pigmented protuberance are visualized during colonoscopy.

Authors of a systematic review of 11 nonrandomized trials of 700 patients with a diagnosis of colonic bleeding found that endoscopic treatment was the most performed initial approach for continued bleeding (66% of all treated patients).

In one case series of 64 patients, endoscopic clipping was reported to have a 75% success rate for primary hemostasis; five of the patients (21%) with stigmata of recent hemorrhage who received clip treatment had rebleeding at 43 months. In another case series of 29 patients with 31 diverticula with stigmata of recent hemorrhage, 27 colonic diverticula were successfully banded (87%). Early rebleeding rate was 11%.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 16 studies with 384 patients with colonic diverticular bleeding found that ligation therapy was more effective than clipping in avoiding need for embolization or surgery and marginally lower than coagulation (rates 0% [95% CI 0.0-0.01], 0.08% [95% CI 0.03-0.16] and 0.18 [95% CI 0.0-0.61], respectively).

A systematic review of 16 studies with 790 participants demonstrated that early rebleeding (8% vs. 19%, p = 0.01) and late rebleeding (9% vs. 29%, p = 0.02) were both less likely with band ligation than with clipping.
Therapeutic colonoscopy was found to be superior to medical therapy in terms of the rate of rebleeding and length of hospital stay.
If colonoscopy fails to reveal source of bleeding or is unavailable, then consider CTA to localize bleeding prior to arteriography or surgery.
Intra-arterial vasopressin infusion during arteriography is 90% effective in controlling bleeding but 50% of patients rebleed and this method is rarely used in clinical practice.
Selective arteriography with therapeutic embolization is 76% to 100% effective in controlling bleeding.
Embolization of bleeding vessel is a definitive means of controlling bleeding, but intestinal infarction may occur in about 20% of patients.
A consensus statement from attendees of the 2nd International Symposium on Diverticular Disease of the Colon is to use selective angiography for massive bleeding.
See .
Most (85%) diverticular bleeding is self-limited. C
Blood loss is massive and rapid in 9% to 19% of patients. C
Recurrent bleeding is often an indication to consider surgical intervention. C
Bleeding stops spontaneously in 85% of patients.

In the systematic review of 11 nonrandomized studies noted above, only 16% (7.6%-100%) of patients with colonic bleeding needed an interventional treatment. Of the 114 patients requiring intervention, 2.2% to 30.4% underwent emergency surgery (total 28/114, 24.5%).
Rebleeding rates range from 13% to 48%, chance of third rebleeding episode is as high as 50%.

In the UK study of 2528 patients with lower GI bleeding, 13.6% of patients rebled during hospital admission and 4.4% were readmitted with bleeding within 28 days. In-hospital mortality was 85/2528 (3.4%) and was higher in patients experiencing rebleeding (7.1%) and in established inpatients (17.8%).

In one retrospective study of 72 patients with diverticular bleeding, risk factors for rebleeding (occurred in 38%) based on multivariate analysis were nonsteroid anti-inflammatory drugs (hazard ratio [HR]; 2.57; 95% CI 0.89-7.5), antiplatelet drugs (HR 2.39; 95% CI 1.01-5.7) and hypertension (HR 4.16; 95% CI 1.22-14.2). Obesity is also a possible risk factor for rebleeding.
In two other cohort studies, age >70 years and presence of shock on admission were additional clinical risk factors for rebleeding.
Most patients (75%-80%) with diverticulosis will remain asymptomatic.
Surgical mortality is approximately 10% to 20% in patients with uncontrolled bleeding requiring emergency surgery.
In one study using the 2008 Nationwide Inpatient Sample, transferred patients had higher in-hospital mortality rates compared to primarily admitted patients (3.5% vs. 1.8%; OR 1.8; 95% CI 1.5-2.8).
No treatment or follow-up is necessary for patients with asymptomatic diverticulosis.
Surveillance colonoscopy is not recommended unless it is performed for other indications, such as colorectal cancer screening.
